# Log-normalized concave weights: compactness and sampled polyhedrality

This note independently proves the bounded ingredients of the contributor's new logarithmic parameter setting. It distinguishes genuine fixed-epsilon attainment from the false compactness of a fixed number of positive affine planes. The closed parameter class permits nonnegative upper-semicontinuous concave weights, positive on each sampled fiber interior; continuity at every boundary point is NOT asserted by the compactness argument.

The original cardinality-minimal bad-base body compactness and strict proper-minor quota theorem remain dependencies. No Gamma payment is derived.

Weights that agree on all sampled fiber interiors have the same normalization and buffered objective. For compactness we select their CANONICAL concave roof from the sampled hypographs. Original concavity ensures this roof reproduces the sampled values. This choice is necessary: arbitrary concave extensions can have unbounded bumps between sampled bases that the mixed measure never sees. Compactness is claimed for these canonical representatives, not for every unsampled extension.

## 1. Two planes do not compactify inverse-power parameters

Already on K=[0,1], d=1, r=2, put 0<e<1 and

    H_e(x)=min(1,e+x/e^2),
    I_e=integral_0^1 H_e^(-2)=1+e(1-e)^2,
    L_e=sqrt(I_e) H_e.

These are the minimum of TWO positive affine planes, and integral L_e^(-2)=1. Nevertheless L_e(0)=e sqrt(I_e) tends to zero. On each fixed [delta,1], L_e is eventually the constant sqrt(I_e), which tends to one. The transition layer has width e^2(1-e), and its inverse-square mass tends to zero. Thus there is no uniformly positive parameter limit, even with fixed body and two planes.

The buffered objectives also converge to the constant-parameter objective. The interval energy is E(x)=4x(1-x). Outside the layer only the scalar sqrt(I_e) changes; inside, E<=4e^2. Hence sqrt(L_e E) converges UNIFORMLY to sqrt(E). The all-normal slab estimate therefore gives uniform buffered-depth convergence.

This disproves literal positive-parameter compactness of fixed finite-plane sublevels. It does not disprove infimum attainment after deleting inessential planes, nor a structural finite-plane conclusion at an already attained minimum. For a general fixed exponent r>1 one can use H=min(1,e+A x), A=e^(-r), with exact inverse moment

    integral H^(-r)
       =1+[e^(1-r)-1]/[A(r-1)]-(1-e)/A ->1.

For r=1 take A=e^(-1); the logarithmic layer term log(1/e)/A also tends to zero. Convergence here concerns the CHOSEN exponent, not all higher inverse moments.

## 2. A logarithmic normalization bound for arbitrary concave weights

Let K be a positive d-body and L>=0 concave and upper semicontinuous on K, positive in its interior. Let m=max_K L>0. If v is a maximizing point, concavity gives

    |{L>=t m}|>=(1-t)^d |K|,       0<=t<=1.

Indeed (1-t)K+t v lies in that superlevel. Layer integration yields

    log m-H_d <= |K|^(-1) integral_K log L <= log m,     (1)

where H_d=sum_(j=1)^d 1/j. Also integral_K L>=m |K|/(d+1), and Jensen at the ordinary centroid g gives

    L(g)>=m/(d+1).                                      (2)

Now let L be jointly concave on the canonical finite fiber hull, and set m_z=max_(K_z)L(z,.). The array m is sampled-concave: select maximizing points in any anchored input relation, combine them into the actual target fiber, and use concavity of L. Under geometric normalization

    sum_z w_z |K_z|^(-1) integral_(K_z) log L=0,

equation (1) gives

    0<=sum_z w_z log m_z<=H_d.                          (3)

## 3. Bad sublevels bound all fiber maxima above and below

Normalize the actual bodies by the established original bad-sublevel theorem: M=1, all V_z>=v>0, bounded fibers, and strict closed-minor quotas at every limit. Let A=sum_z w_z m_z.

If A tended to infinity, h_z=m_z/A would have a convergent nonnegative sampled-concave subsequence of weighted mean one. Its positive limit set U satisfies the exact midpoint positivity property of the audited concave-array arithmetic theorem. That theorem supplies a fixed p in U whose limiting atomic base depth is at least 1/k(P). At that base m_p tends to infinity, and (2) forces L(p,g_p) to infinity. Positive centroid energy and covariance then make its buffered depth equal atomic depth, contradicting a fixed bad sublevel b<Gamma_d/k(P).

Thus A is bounded above. Since w_z>=v, all m_z have a common finite upper bound. The lower inequality in (3), together with that upper bound and the positive weights, bounds each m_z away from zero. This step uses logarithmic normalization essentially; no inverse-power boundary divergence is invoked.

## 4. Interior compactness, logarithmic uniform integrability and depth

For a convex body of diameter at most D and an interior point X,

    L(X)>=m dist(X,boundary K)/D.                       (4)

Extend the segment from a maximizing point through X to the far boundary. The coefficient of the maximizing endpoint is at least dist(X,boundary K)/D, and concavity with nonnegative boundary values proves (4).

The compact positive body family has common interior-ball radii. Its boundary layers satisfy uniformly

    |{X in K:dist(X,boundary K)<=s}|<=C s

for small s: an inner homothetic copy about an inball center lies in the inner parallel body. Consequently (4) and the uniform upper/lower bounds on m give uniform integrability of log L, with the negative boundary-layer contribution bounded by C' s(1+|log s|).

Bounded concave functions are uniformly Lipschitz on every common interior core. A diagonal subsequence therefore converges locally uniformly on each limiting sampled fiber interior, to a positive concave function there. Take its upper-semicontinuous concave closure at the boundary. Exact anchored inequalities pass to these limits: first use interior input points, whose convex combination lies in the target interior because the inputs contain small balls, then approximate boundary inputs and use upper semicontinuity. The canonical concave roof of these sampled hypographs supplies a genuine jointly concave weight on the limiting canonical body and reproduces the sampled values. This roof is bounded by the maximum of the sampled fiber maxima. That bound would be false for an arbitrary extension above the canonical roof.

Uniform logarithmic integrability proves convergence of the mixed log integrals, so normalization survives. This is not a claim that the weights converge uniformly at all boundary points.

For the actual buffers, that difficulty disappears. On interior cores, L_j and the energies converge uniformly. Near a fiber boundary, L_j remains bounded while E_j tends uniformly to zero under positive-body Hausdorff convergence. Hence

    f_j=[L_j E_j/M_j]^(1/(d+1))

converges uniformly on the sampled fibers, with zero boundary extension. Mixed-measure symmetric differences, covariance continuity and the all-direction slab estimate now give buffered-depth and maximal-depth convergence. Base tilts introduce no extra error in that estimate.

Thus the contributor's proposed nonnegative concave logarithmic parameter class has fixed-epsilon bad-sublevel sequential compactness in this physically relevant topology, and the joint infimum is attained whenever the original bad reference gives a strict sublevel. The conclusion is for the enlarged upper-semicontinuous class; closed-body continuous weights alone have not been proved compact by this argument.

## 5. Finite affine majorants on the SAMPLED fibers

Let L be any member of this class and let (p,y) be an own-interior mark. A finite full-space affine majorant touching there need not dominate L at every real base: continuous concavity alone can have infinite base slopes at a projection boundary. What is always available is a majorant on the sampled fibers, which is sufficient for all integrals and normalization.

Choose a continuous-coordinate supergradient g of L(p,.) at y. It exists at an interior point. Set

    phi_z=max_(X in K_z)[L(z,X)-g·X].

This finite array is sampled-concave, by actual anchored inclusion and joint concavity. At p it equals L(p,y)-g·y. The finite support LP for a sampled-concave array supplies a base affine majorant touching phi at p. Consequently there is a full-space affine A with

    A>=L on every sampled fiber,   A(p,y)=L(p,y).       (5)

Since A is nonnegative on the sampled fibers, it is nonnegative on their entire convex hull. It is strictly positive on every sampled fiber INTERIOR, but may vanish at its boundary. No stronger positivity is asserted here.

## 6. Sampled polyhedrality at an attained unpenalized minimum

Assume a genuine joint unpenalized local minimum below 1/k(P), now over this entire concave logarithmic class. Atomic hinge cleanup gives at least one proper deepest base. As before there is at most one proper deepest mark in a given base: strict fixed-fiber energy-root concavity, combined with positive concavity of L, makes the buffer strictly concave, and an attained proper cap at the midpoint would force equality if two such marks existed.

Choose ONE majorant (5) for each proper deepest mark and put T=min_i A_i. It is a nonnegative concave finite-plane weight, positive on sampled fiber interiors, majorizes L on S, and equals L at every proper mark. It need NOT majorize L at every nonsampled real base. Nevertheless

    L_raw,t=(1-t)L+tT

is jointly concave and nonnegative, and is a legal raw path. Its logarithmic normalization factor is

    c_t=exp[-<log L_raw,t>].

If T>L on a set of positive mixed volume, put D=T-L on S. The quantity D_norm(t)=<log(1+tD/L)> has D_norm(t)/t tending to <D/L> in (0,infinity], by monotone convergence. Choose a>0 so D_norm(t)>=2at for small t. Since D/L is continuous near the proper marks and vanishes at every one, choose one neighborhood on which D/L<=a. There

    log[c_t L_raw,t/L]
      =-D_norm(t)+log(1+tD/L)<=-at<0.

Also D_norm(t) tends to zero by integrability of log L and boundedness of T, so the buffered depths converge uniformly to the old ones. Outside the chosen neighborhood the old strict gap persists. The established strict own-strip comparison lowers the whole proper-base maxima. Atomic bases remain bounded by their unchanged base caps and, if necessary, an actual all-atomic hinge step supplies strict descent. In this cleanup the fixed old concave weight is restricted to the eroded bodies and logarithmically renormalized; absolute integrability of its old logarithm makes this normalization continuous under the shrinking removed sets.

Therefore every such chosen T equals L almost everywhere on S. Interior continuity then gives equality on every sampled fiber INTERIOR. Replacing boundary values and the nonsampled extension by T changes neither mixed normalization nor sampled buffered depth, since E vanishes on own fiber boundaries. At a globally attained minimum this gives an equivalent globally minimizing finite-plane representative with at most |J| planes.

The path argument does not claim compactness before attainment; Section 1 rules out that shortcut. It also does not yet exclude zeros of those nonnegative planes. That is the separate body-cut/logarithmic-gain mechanism the contributor is analyzing.

## 7. Finite reciprocal moment at an attained bad minimum

There is one additional exact parameter-only consequence. At such a minimum,

    <1/L><infinity.                                    (6)

If not, add a constant t>0 and normalize:

    D(t)=<log(1+t/L)>,
    L_t=exp[-D(t)](L+t).

Integrability of log L makes D(t) tend to zero, whereas monotone convergence gives D(t)/t tending to infinity. On a fixed interior neighborhood of all proper marks, L has a positive lower bound, so exp[-D(t)](1+t/L)<1 for small t. The same gap/strip/atomic-cleanup argument gives a strict descent. This proves (6) without pretending that negative affine directions are legal at boundary zeros.

Finite (6) alone does not supply equal-mass full-space martingale marginals: the tangent cone still has boundary constraints. Removing those constraints requires an actual exclusion of zeros, not merely differentiating the normalization.
